title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

title: GLARE: Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification
abstract: Reliable classification of transposable elements (TEs) is important for genome annotation and evolutionary analysis, yet remains challenging: TE families differ widely across taxa, reference databases label them inconsistently, and many TEs are represented only by degraded copies. We introduce GLARE (Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification), a TE classifier built by fine-tuning a genomic language model on harmonized PanTEon and Repbase reference data to predict TE superfamily across 32 superfamilies in 11 orders. Among the genomic language models compared, Nucleotide Transformer v3 provided the strongest representation. Built on this backbone, GLARE exceeded all nine classifiers in the PanTEon benchmark, reaching 0.966 weighted superfamily F1 on its 30-superfamily task. GLARE also showed stronger generalization to clades absent from training, consistently exceeding state-of-the-art classifiers on holdouts spanning three taxonomic ranks: the order Poales, the phylum Arthropoda, and the kingdom Fungi. Training on both PanTEon and Repbase reduced the performance drop seen when a single-source model was applied to the other database. Under simulated sequence decay, GLARE was the most robust classifier tested, and it performed best on independently curated degraded libraries. These findings show that genomic language models fine-tuned on harmonized multi-source references can classify TEs robustly under the taxonomic, database, and sequence-quality shifts that matter in practice. GLARE is available at https://code.jgi.doe.gov/NHaas/glare.

title: ClinStigma: A Clinician-Guided Framework for Developing Synthetic Benchmarks of Contextual Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation
abstract: Objective Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, summarize, and evaluate clinical documentation, yet standardized methods for evaluating nuanced, context-dependent clinical language remain limited. Existing approaches rely primarily on annotated clinical corpora or keyword-based methods, restricting reproducibility, public dissemination, and systematic comparison across models. We present ClinStigma, a clinician-guided framework for constructing, annotating, and evaluating synthetic benchmarks of contextual stigmatizing language, demonstrated through ClinStigma-SUD, its inaugural implementation for substance use disorder documentation. Materials and Methods Candidate clinical sentences were generated using a frontier language model and iteratively reviewed according to a clinician-developed annotation rubric refined through expert review in stigmatizing language. The resulting benchmark intentionally incorporates explicit stigmatizing, neutral, and contextually ambiguous ("gray-zone") documentation requiring clinical reasoning rather than keyword recognition. Three locally deployed open-weight LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot inference, followed by external evaluation using independently annotated clinical documentation from MIMIC-IV. Results ClinStigma-SUD consists of 500 clinician-adjudicated synthetic clinical documentation sentences. Inter-rater agreement was 98.8% across the full benchmark (Cohen's {kappa} = 0.976) and 94.0% within the intentionally ambiguous subset ({kappa} = 0.880). Under zero-shot prompting, binary accuracy ranged from 84.8% to 91.8% across evaluated models, while F1 for the ambiguous (gray) class ranged from 0.038 to 0.423. Zero-shot external evaluation on 3,716 annotated examples from the independently annotated Harrigian MIMIC-IV corpus yielded 84.4% accuracy (84.4% balanced accuracy; macro F1 0.824), against a 69.9% majority-class baseline. Stigmatizing-class F1 was 0.879 in the substance-related subgroup and 0.883 in the full external corpus. Discussion and Conclusion ClinStigma establishes a reproducible clinician-guided framework for developing synthetic evaluation benchmarks for contextual clinical language. By combining structured clinical expertise, explicit annotation guidance, synthetic benchmark generation, and external evaluation, the framework enables open, privacy-preserving evaluation of language models while providing a scalable foundation for benchmark development across additional clinical specialties, including obstetrics, emergency medicine, and mental health.

title: UniMedSeg: Unified Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation via Uncertainty Guided Encoding and Frequency-Spatial Dual-Prompt Decoding
abstract: Text-driven medical image segmentation demands unified models based on multi-modal learning, capable of processing diverse imaging modalities while providing spatially reliable prediction estimates for clinical practice. Nevertheless, existing vision-language model solutions suffer from poor domain generalization and exhibit limited capability for uncertainty estimation to model the cumulative unreliability of cross-modal alignment across network layers. In this paper, we propose UniMedSeg, a unified vision-language framework for multi-modal medical image segmentation built upon frozen pre-trained vision-language backbones. Our framework incorporates modality-aware adaptation, cross-layer uncertainty-guided encoding, and a frequency-spatial dual-prompt decoder, wherein the progressive uncertainty propagation mechanism of the encoder suppresses misleading cross-modal features, whereas the decoder disentangles anatomical structure and boundary details in the frequency domain under dual textual prompts. Auxiliary losses further sharpen boundary representations and calibrate pixel-wise uncertainty maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniMedSeg preserves competitive in-domain segmentation performance, improves domain generalization, and yields clinically useful spatial risk estimation.

title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

title: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
abstract: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

title: Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
abstract: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.

title: Global statistical constraint and local partner-sensitive inference support dynamic, open-ended verbal coordination
abstract: Effective verbal communication requires individuals to align their communicative intentions through the precise use of utterances, yet how this is achieved in dynamic, open-ended communication remains unclear. Combining predictive deep language models (DLMs) with cognitive computational modeling, we tested a computational division of labor between context-sensitive global constraint on the utterance space and partner-sensitive local adjustment of selection priorities. We formalized local adjustment using an active inference inspired updating rule within a statistical-pragmatic hybrid model. Thirty dyads performed a dynamic, open-ended collaborative word-generation task during functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning. Interlocutors converged in their lexical choices, and lexical alignment was best explained by a hybrid model integrating contextual selection priors with interaction-specific local adjustment among the models tested. This hybrid process formed a dynamic hypothesis landscape comprising a global semantic search region and local selection priorities. Critically, interaction did not simply reduce uncertainty: within individuals, the hypothesis space of global semantic search progressively narrowed while local uncertainty among plausible alternatives increased; between partners, both global hypothesis space and local selection became increasingly aligned, with alignment of local selection priorities most strongly predicting subsequent lexical alignment. The contribution of local adjustment was stronger during precise verbal communication than in the control tasks. Neural analyses further identified correlates of the local adjustment process: temporoparietal and anterior temporal regions supported partner-related inference and semantic prediction error, respectively, and their activity during thinking predicted subsequent inferior frontal activity associated with self-updating during speaking. The participant's own hypothesis landscape was also represented in the left inferior parietal-supramarginal cortex. The main findings generalized across language models and an independent Czech dataset. Together, these findings reveal that alignment in open-ended communication emerges from complementary statistical and pragmatic computations, providing a framework for understanding human and human-AI communication.

title: Dementia Language Models: a generalizable and controllable representation of cognitive impairment
abstract: We introduce Dementia Language Models (DeLMs)--generalizable and controllable representations of cognitive impairment through language--alongside an evaluation framework for establishing their validity and clinical grounding. DeLMs created by fine-tuning large language models on a small clinical corpus successfully generated patient-like narratives across unseen tasks, received predicted Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores in the impaired range, and produced narratives that neurologists identified with accuracy comparable to real transcripts. The models' internal representations, as well as their non-linguistic decision-making, supported mild cognitive impairment detection in unseen cohorts. The effect was controllable: moving from Healthy toward Dementia in weight space progressively worsened language and predicted MMSE scores while increasing dementia probability. DeLMs could support clinician training, hypothesis generation, and scalable experimentation, reserving patient involvement for where it is truly needed.

title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry
abstract: On real-world dental records, procedure history predicts the next procedure category well, and a simple history-aware classical model beats every large-language-model (LLM) design we tested. We study the question that follows every dental diagnosis: given a patients chart and most recent procedure, what should the dentist do next? Commercial dental artificial intelligence in 2026 is overwhelmingly diagnostic, and the closest published system for this sequencing task, MultiTP (Chen et al., 2024b), offers neither calibrated uncertainty, structured rationale, nor an evaluation as decision support. We introduce DentaCoPilot, a recommender that returns a calibrated top-K distribution over Current Dental Terminology (CDT) codes, a verbalised confidence label, an explicit abstain flag, and a chart-grounded rationale, and we compare four classical baselines with six LLM variants. On an apples-to-apples synthetic evaluation, classical baselines reach 0.567 top-1 while pure LLM variants trail at 0.267 to 0.467, and moving the backbone from Sonnet to Opus does not help. Prompt-conditioning a Sonnet LLM on the classical baselines candidate list closes most of the gap while preserving rationale and abstention; because the synthetic generator shares Markov structure with the bigram baseline, these synthetic rankings index pipeline behaviour, not externally valid clinical performance. We anchor external validity for the task on the public MEPS 2023 corpus (11,016 next-visit transitions across 5,088 patients): a history-aware model reaches 0.479 top-1 against 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.031), and supports split-conformal selective prediction with a distribution-free coverage guarantee. A zero-shot LLM given only 1 this coarse history loses to the same classical baseline, so the LLMs value depends on rich charts rather than category history alone. Prospective clinician-in-the-loop validation and CDT-level real-data validation remain future work, contingent on clinical-data access and ethics approval that we have sought but not secured.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Prediction and Diagnosis of Fetal Growth Restriction: A Systematic Review.
abstract: This systematic review evaluates evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for prediction and diagnosis of fetal growth restriction (FGR). The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, through June 2026 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies on AI/ML-based prediction or diagnosis techniques for FGR, Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) or Small for gestational age (SGA) fetuses. The prediction model risk of bias assessment Tool (PROBAST) was used to perform data extraction and risk of bias assessment. Twenty-seven studies were eligible for inclusion. AI applications were biophysical (n = 10), Doppler-based (n = 10), clinical (n = 7), ultrasound (n = 7), MRI (n = 7), radiomics imaging (n = 10), cardiotocography (n = 10), genomics (n = 10), and metabolomics-based biomarker models (n = 10). The model performance was good, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC) of 0.71-0.91 and classification accuracies of 78.9-93.3%. Imaging and multimodal data-based models showed the highest predictive performance. The PROBAST assessment showed that the risk of bias was low for the participant, predictor and outcome domains, but the analytical domain raised methodological concerns; nine studies were low risk, 14 moderate and 4 high. The AI and ML models for FGR detection performed promisingly. Multimodal approaches that combine clinical, imaging and molecular data consistently outperform single modality models and constitute a major advance in precision obstetrics. However, there remains substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation and methodological issues. Future prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and real-world implementation research are needed for routine clinical adoption.

title: Artificial intelligence in human microbiome research: from data integration to explainable translation.
abstract: The human microbiome is integral to health, metabolism, immunity, and physical protection, with dysbiosis linked to metabolic disorders, autoimmune conditions, and cancer. High-throughput sequencing has generated massive datasets, but analyzing these complex, multidimensional data poses significant challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, and related approaches, offers powerful solutions for data integration, pattern recognition, functional annotation, and predictive modeling. AI applications in microbiome research include identifying microbial biomarkers, predicting disease susceptibility, elucidating microbial interactions, and optimizing personalized interventions. AI also enables integration of microbiome data with host genomics, transcriptomics, and clinical metadata, providing a holistic view of host-microbiome dynamics. Despite advances, challenges such as data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and limited sample sizes remain. This narrative review synthesizes literature from 2015 to 2025 without a formal systematic methodology. We conclude with three priority areas for AI-microbiome translation: improved interpretability, longitudinal modeling, and clinical integration. Leveraging AI in this field holds significant promise for accelerating precision medicine, improving diagnostics, and developing microbiome-targeted therapies, if interpretability and validation challenges are addressed.

title: CodonBench: separating gene context, exon position, and variant-specific component in synonymous-variant classification
abstract: Background. A synonymous variant leaves the protein unchanged, so a classifier that still separates pathogenic from benign examples must be reading something beyond the protein. Such variants test cleanly what a codon-level model adds to a protein-level one. Methods. We assembled SynPath, a benchmark of ClinVar synonymous variants, and scored frozen representations under two splitting protocols. Under gene-held-out folds whole genes are withheld, and each coding-sequence model is compared against a position-matched control. Results. The models were not trained for this task, so these numbers describe transfer, not designed performance. Random splitting flatters every representation. Once whole genes are held out, they fall into a narrow band near chance, the best at 0.58, and low-rank fine-tuning does not restore the random-split level. A feature that reads no sequence, only the distance from the variant to the nearest exon junction, reaches 0.84 under the same folds, above every neural representation tested. In a protein model the variant-specific component is zero by construction, because both alleles present the same input. In coding-sequence models only the response vector, the difference between the alternate and reference embeddings, keeps signal on unseen genes and beats its position-matched control. Conclusions. Synonymous-variant pathogenicity is predictable mainly from gene identity and from position. Only a small part reflects the variant itself, and only in models that read the coding sequence. Benchmarks judged on random splits will overstate what these models have learned.

title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
abstract: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.
